opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those things where the representation choices end up mattering a lot more than people expect, mostly because MCTS is going to touch these objects millions of times.

For the state, the simplest version is just the board: a 19x19 grid where each intersection is empty, black, or white. But the board alone isn't actually a complete state in Go. You also need whose turn it is, and you need enough history to enforce the ko rule, so you can't just immediately recapture and repeat a position. If you're doing superko you technically need the whole set of prior positions, which is usually handled with Zobrist hashing: you assign a random 64-bit number to each (intersection, color) pair and XOR them together, so you get a cheap incremental hash of the position you can check against a set.

Then there's the neural network's view of the state, which is a bit different from the game engine's view. In the AlphaGo Zero style setup, you stack feature planes: one plane for your stones, one for the opponent's stones, repeated over the last eight or so positions, plus a plane indicating the color to play. The history planes help with ko but also, empirically, the network just learns better with some temporal context. You always encode it from the perspective of the player to move, so the network doesn't have to learn two separate games.

For actions, Go is nice because the action space is small and fixed: 361 intersections plus a pass move, so 362. The policy head outputs a distribution over those, and you mask out illegal moves, like occupied points, suicide, and ko violations, then renormalize.

On the tree side, the key design decision is that the statistics live on the edges, not the nodes. Each edge, meaning a state-action pair, stores a visit count N, a total value W, the mean value Q, and the prior P from the policy network. Selection uses PUCT, roughly Q plus a term proportional to P times the square root of the parent's visit count over one plus the child's count. That's how the prior from the network steers exploration toward plausible moves without you having to expand all 362 children by brute force.

A practical detail: you lazily expand. When you hit a leaf, you run the network once, get the priors and a value estimate, create the edges, and back the value up the path, flipping the sign at each level because it's a two-player zero-sum game. You don't store full board copies in every node if you can avoid it; you can replay moves from the root or store compact representations, because memory blows up quickly otherwise.

And one thing I'd emphasize: exploiting symmetry. A Go board has eight symmetries, rotations and reflections, and you can randomly transform the input before evaluation or average across them. It's basically free data augmentation and makes the value estimates more robust.

So the short version is: the game-engine state needs to be exact and hashable for rules, the network state needs to be a rich, player-relative tensor, and the action representation is a flat 362-way vector with legality masking, with all the search statistics hanging off the edges.

r001.rationale: The response says edges store state-action statistics and describes a separate 362-action representation. It does not explain that an action can be represented implicitly by the transition from parent to child without storing it separately.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the first thing I'd say is that the state representation question is actually two questions that people tend to conflate. There's the representation the tree search uses to identify and hash a node, and there's the representation you feed to the network to get a policy and value. Those don't have to be the same thing, and in practice they shouldn't be.

For the tree itself, the thing you care about is: given a sequence of moves, can I cheaply tell whether I've been here before, and can I generate the legal successors. So for Go the canonical move is Zobrist hashing. You assign a random 64-bit number to every (intersection, color) pair, and the hash of a position is just the XOR of all the stones on the board, plus a bit for who's to move. The beautiful thing is that it's incremental. Placing a stone is one XOR, capturing a group is a handful of XORs. You never recompute the whole board. And you get ko detection for free, because superko is just "have I seen this hash before in the history of this line," which is a set lookup. So the node in the tree is really just a hash, a visit count, a sum of values, and a prior over children. That's maybe a few dozen bytes per node, which matters a lot when you're expanding hundreds of thousands of nodes per move.

Then the network representation is a totally different design problem. The AlphaGo-style answer is a stack of 19 by 19 binary planes: your stones, their stones, that repeated for the last eight moves so the network can see ko and recent captures, plus a plane that's all ones or all zeros for side to move. The thing I'd emphasize is that the history planes are doing real work. Go is technically Markov given the full superko history, but a single board snapshot isn't, and more importantly the recent history is an incredibly strong prior on where the action is. People sometimes try to drop it to save compute and the policy gets noticeably worse.

The other thing that I think is underappreciated is symmetry. The Go board has eight symmetries, rotations and reflections, and you want your value estimates to be invariant to them. The cheap trick is you just randomly pick one of the eight transforms every time you call the network from inside the search, and average implicitly over many evaluations. That's basically free regularization, and it also means the policy priors in the tree are less biased by whatever quirks the network learned about, you know, the top left corner specifically.

On the action side, it's pretty clean in Go because the action space is small and discrete: 361 intersections plus pass. So the policy head is just a 362-way softmax and the tree's edges index directly into that. Where it gets interesting is what you do with illegal moves. You have to mask them before you normalize, because if you don't, a meaningful chunk of your prior mass can sit on moves that can't happen, and then your PUCT exploration term is miscalibrated. People get subtly wrong search behavior from that and it's hard to diagnose because nothing crashes.

And then the pass move deserves special attention. Early in training, networks love to pass, because passing is always legal and the value signal is noisy. If your tree lets passing be an ordinary action with an ordinary prior, you'll get a lot of games that end absurdly early. So there's usually some handling there, either a resign threshold or a rule that you only consider passing once the opponent has passed or the board is settled.

The last point I'd make is more philosophical. The reason this works for Go and is much harder for, say, robotics, is that in Go the state is fully observable, the dynamics are known and deterministic, and the action space is tiny and discrete. So you can afford to represent the state exactly and spend all your modeling capacity on the value function. When I think about MCTS for continuous control, almost every one of those assumptions breaks. You don't know the dynamics, so you need a learned model, and now the node in your tree is a latent vector rather than a hash. You can't enumerate actions, so you're sampling them, and progressive widening becomes the whole game. The Go version is clean enough that it's worth really understanding, because it's sort of the platonic ideal that everything else is a corruption of.

r001.rationale: The response says tree edges index directly into the 362-action policy and discusses moves as explicit actions. It does not explain that an action can be represented implicitly by the transition from a parent state to its child without storing it separately.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by separating the game state from the search statistics. The state contains the board configuration, whose turn it is, and enough history to determine whether a move is legal. In Go, the board alone isn’t always sufficient, because ko or superko rules depend on previous positions.

An action is usually placing a stone at a particular intersection, or passing. So on a 19-by-19 board, you can represent that as 361 positions plus a pass action, and mask out illegal moves. Applying an action produces a new state: you place the stone, remove captured stones, and update the player and the relevant history.

Then the search tree stores things like visit counts and estimated values for each state-action edge. If you’re using a neural network to guide the search, you also store its prior probability for each move. Those statistics are properties of the search, rather than part of the Go position itself.

One subtle implementation detail is being consistent about whose perspective a value represents. A position that’s good for me is bad for you, so when you back up values through alternating turns, you need to handle that sign change correctly.

r001.rationale: The response represents actions explicitly as board positions or pass actions and discusses statistics for each state-action edge. It does not say an action can be represented implicitly by the parent-to-child transition without storing it separately.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d represent a state as the board position plus whatever information you need to determine legal moves and how the game continues. So that includes whose turn it is, the ko situation, and enough history to enforce the repetition rule you’re using. The board by itself isn’t necessarily the full state.

An action is pretty simple: place a stone at a particular intersection, or pass. On a 19-by-19 board, you can encode that as 361 possible placements plus one pass action, and mask out the illegal placements.

Then, in the search tree, a node represents a state, and an outgoing edge represents an action. You typically keep the visit count and estimated value for each edge, and, if you have a policy network, its prior probability for that move. One thing you have to be careful about is the value convention: is this value from Black’s perspective, or from the perspective of the player about to move? Either works, but the backup operation has to be consistent about it.

For efficiency, you don’t necessarily need to store a complete board at every node. You can keep a board that supports playing and undoing moves as you traverse the tree. That’s an implementation choice; the conceptual distinction is still that states describe positions and actions describe the choices available from those positions.

r001.rationale: The response says an outgoing edge represents an action and describes actions as explicit moves. It does not explain that the transition from parent state to child state can represent the action without storing it separately.
